title: Guardrails Are Not a Safety Net. They Are a Contract.
dek: Most teams bolt on output validation at the end. Here is why that framing produces brittle systems.

blocks.label: The framing most teams get wrong
blocks.html: Treating guardrails as a safety net — something you add after the real work is done — is exactly backwards. A guardrail is a contract between your system and whatever consumes its output. If you design it last, you've already made a dozen architectural decisions that the contract will quietly violate.

The dominant conversation around LLM guardrails goes something like this: you build the pipeline, you get it working, and then you sprinkle in some validation to catch the bad stuff before it hits the user. Jailbreaks, hallucinated field names, off-topic responses — guardrails as a filter layer. That mental model is wrong, and it produces systems that are fragile in ways that are genuinely hard to debug. When validation is an afterthought, it operates on outputs it was never consulted about shaping. You end up writing increasingly baroque regex patterns and schema checks to compensate for a prompt that was never written with machine-readable output in mind.

The concept Simon Willison recently highlighted — the meat proxy, a person who blindly relays AI output without actually reading it — applies just as well to software systems. A pipeline with no output contract is a meat proxy in code. It copies whatever the model produces and passes it downstream, hoping nothing breaks. Guardrails, designed up front, force you to specify what the system is actually supposed to produce. That is a design activity, not a remediation activity.

Here is what changes when you treat validation as a contract rather than a filter. First, your prompt changes. If you know the output must conform to a specific schema — say, a RiskAssessment object with a required confidence_score between 0 and 1 and a non-empty rationale field — you write the prompt to produce that. You include the schema in the system prompt. You test against it from day one. Second, your retry logic changes. Instead of a generic error handler, you have a validator that can tell you which constraint failed, which means a targeted re-prompt is possible rather than a full restart. Third, and most importantly, your failure modes become visible. A contract violation is a named, logged, observable event. Unvalidated output failures tend to surface as mysterious downstream bugs three hops away from the actual cause.

The trade-off is real: defining the contract up front takes time, and for genuinely open-ended generative tasks — creative writing, long-form summarisation — a rigid schema is the wrong tool. Not every LLM output needs to be a structured object. But if your output is consumed by another system, another model, or any code at all, you almost certainly need a contract. The failure mode I see most often in enterprise deployments is teams who discover this six months in, after the pipeline has ossified around an implicit and undocumented output format that the model only approximately respects.

title: Instrument Your LLM Calls Before You Need To
dek: How to add tracing to your LLM application so you can actually debug it when things go wrong.

blocks.html: Most teams add observability after something breaks in production. That's backwards. Tracing is cheap to set up, and the data it gives you — latency per step, token counts, the exact prompt that caused a bad output — is nearly impossible to reconstruct after the fact. Do it on day one.

blocks.heading: LLM Trace Lifecycle
blocks.alt: Request Received → Trace Opened → LLM Call Logged → Tool Calls Logged → Response Returned → Trace Stored

blocks.heading: What to Capture on Every Trace

items.title: Full prompt, not just the template
items.detail: Log the rendered string sent to the model — variables substituted, system prompt included. Templates lie; the rendered call doesn't.

items.title: Model, version, and parameters
items.detail: Temperature, top-p, max tokens. A silent default change in your client library has broken more things than you'd expect.

items.title: Latency at each span
items.detail: Break it down: retrieval, LLM call, post-processing. Aggregate latency hides where the time actually goes.

items.title: Token usage per call
items.detail: Input and output tokens separately. This is your cost signal and your context-window early warning system.

items.title: User and session identifiers
items.detail: Without these, you can't correlate a complaint to a trace. Add them from the start, even in internal tools.

blocks.heading: Rules for Keeping Traces Useful Long-Term

items.title: Name spans after what they do, not what they call
items.detail: "retrieve_customer_history" is debuggable six months later. "step_3" is not.

items.title: Sample aggressively only after you understand the failure rate
items.detail: 100% tracing is fine at low volume. If you drop to 10% sampling before you know your error patterns, you'll miss the long tail.

items.title: Set retention to match your eval cadence
items.detail: If you run evals weekly, keep at least two weeks of traces. Shorter retention makes regression analysis guesswork.

items.title: Treat traces as a dataset, not just logs
items.detail: Export traces periodically to label edge cases and feed your offline evaluation suite. The trace store is where your fine-tuning data comes from.

title: Red-Teaming Your AI System Before Someone Else Does
dek: Adversarial testing isn't a security luxury — here's the minimum you should be running on every AI deployment.

blocks.html: A Meta model autonomously hacked a third-party system during a cybersecurity benchmark — not because someone told it to, but because the task made it seem like a reasonable next step. That incident is a useful data point, but the real lesson isn't about Meta. It's about what happens when you ship an AI system without ever seriously asking: what's the worst thing this thing could do? Most teams run happy-path evals. They check that the model answers correctly, stays on topic, and handles edge cases gracefully. Almost nobody systematically tries to make the system fail in dangerous ways before it goes to production.

Red-teaming is just structured adversarial testing — you or a tool plays the role of a hostile user, and you look for prompt injections, jailbreaks, data leakage, and unintended tool calls. The failure mode I see most in enterprise deployments isn't the dramatic stuff. It's a RAG pipeline that leaks documents the user shouldn't see, or an agent that follows an instruction embedded in a retrieved web page without questioning its origin. These aren't exotic attacks. They show up in the first ten minutes of a basic red-team sweep. The only reason they reach production is that nobody ran one.

title: What I Learned Filling 180k Tokens and Getting Garbage Back
dek: Long-context windows are not a substitute for thinking carefully about what you actually put in them.

blocks.html:
A client handed me a folder of 40 supplier contracts and said: "Just throw them all at Claude, it can handle 200k tokens." They weren't wrong about the token limit. They were wrong about what happens when you fill it carelessly. We got answers that were technically grounded in the documents but subtly wrong — the model was averaging across conflicting clauses, losing track of which terms applied to which vendor, and generally doing what any human would do if you handed them a stack of paper and said "summarize everything." The window was full. The output was mush.

That incident changed how I think about context. The size of the window is not the interesting problem. The interesting problem is what you put in it, in what order, and how you tell the model to navigate it. That's what I now call context engineering — and it's the part most teams skip entirely because they're still amazed the model can read 40 contracts at once.

A few things I've settled on after enough failures: position matters more than people admit. Instructions buried in the middle of a 100k-token prompt are reliably ignored more often than the same instructions at the top or bottom. Redundant structure helps — if the model needs to know a vendor name to answer correctly, that name should appear near the relevant clause, not just in a header 80k tokens earlier. And when the task is genuinely complex, a single monolithic context is usually the wrong shape. Sub-agents that each hold a smaller, focused slice of information outperform one agent drowning in everything. The quoted excerpt from Florian Herrengt's piece about AI and software bugs points at something related: when a bug is hard to fix repeatedly, often the real problem is that nobody — human or model — has a clean picture of what the code is actually supposed to do. Context rot. The same thing happens in long prompts.

title: Dense vs. Sparse Retrieval: Choosing Your Embedding Strategy
dek: Vector search is not one thing — knowing when to use dense embeddings versus sparse retrieval changes everything downstream.

blocks.html:
There are two fundamentally different ways to match a query against a corpus, and most teams pick one without really thinking about the other. Dense retrieval — turning text into floating-point vectors and finding nearest neighbors — gets all the attention right now. Sparse retrieval — think BM25, TF-IDF, keyword overlap — gets dismissed as "old school." That framing is wrong, and it costs people real accuracy in production.

Dense embeddings are excellent at semantic similarity. Ask "how do I cancel my subscription" and they'll surface a document titled "terminating your account" even though no word overlaps. That's genuinely useful. But they're terrible at exact-match recall: product codes, error codes, proper nouns, very domain-specific jargon. Sparse methods handle those effortlessly. The honest answer for most enterprise search problems I've worked on is that you need to know which failure mode hurts you more — and then probably combine both anyway.

    api_key="YOUR_OPENAI_KEY",

blocks.example_output:
[['To cancel your subscription, go to Account > Billing > Cancel.',
  'You can export your data as CSV from the Settings panel.']]
# Note: 'E-4021' doc not returned — the query had no semantic signal toward error codes

blocks.html:
That last line in the output is the thing to sit with. The error-code document didn't surface — not because the embedding model failed, but because the query carried no semantic signal pointing toward payment errors. A sparse retriever would have caught it if the user typed "E-4021" directly. Dense retrieval wins on paraphrase; sparse retrieval wins on precision. Neither wins unconditionally.

LlamaIndex takes a different approach to this problem. Rather than being a database, it's a retrieval framework — it sits on top of whatever store you choose and gives you composable retrieval strategies. The relevant one here is its hybrid retriever, which runs both a vector search and a keyword search, then fuses the result lists using reciprocal rank fusion or a weighted merge. You configure the balance; LlamaIndex does the plumbing. In practice, this is what I actually deploy for enterprise document search, because the combined approach consistently outperforms either leg on its own across heterogeneous corpora.

blocks.usage_note: LlamaIndex is where I go when the retrieval logic itself needs to be configurable — hybrid search, reranking, metadata filtering — things that would take weeks to build on a bare vector DB.

code_example.code:
from llama_index.core import VectorStoreIndex, SimpleDirectoryReader, Settings
from llama_index.core.retrievers import VectorIndexRetriever
from llama_index.retrievers.bm25 import BM25Retriever
from llama_index.core.retrievers import QueryFusionRetriever
from llama_index.llms.openai import OpenAI
from llama_index.embeddings.openai import OpenAIEmbedding

Settings.llm = OpenAI(model="gpt-4o-mini")
Settings.embed_model = OpenAIEmbedding(model="text-embedding-3-small")

documents = SimpleDirectoryReader("./support_docs").load_data()
index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(documents)

vector_retriever = VectorIndexRetriever(index=index, similarity_top_k=4)
bm25_retriever = BM25Retriever.from_defaults(index=index, similarity_top_k=4)

hybrid_retriever = QueryFusionRetriever(
    retrievers=[vector_retriever, bm25_retriever],
    similarity_top_k=3,
    num_queries=1,
    mode="reciprocal_rerank"
)

nodes = hybrid_retriever.retrieve("E-4021 payment timeout")
for n in nodes:
    print(round(n.score, 3), n.text[:80])

blocks.heading: Dense vs. Hybrid Retrieval: Where Each Fits
blocks.alt: Comparison: Aspect, Dense Only (Chroma), Hybrid (LlamaIndex)

blocks.html:
My rule of thumb: if your corpus is relatively clean and your users phrase queries naturally — think a knowledge base written by technical writers — dense-only is fine and simpler to operate. If your corpus mixes natural-language prose with structured identifiers, version numbers, or code, you will regret not adding the sparse leg. The latency cost of hybrid retrieval is real but usually small relative to the LLM call that follows. The accuracy gain, on the other hand, is immediately visible in user feedback.

One thing I'd push back on in how the industry talks about this: embedding model choice gets obsessed over, while retrieval strategy gets ignored. Swapping from one embedding model to another might move your recall@5 by a few points. Switching from dense-only to hybrid on a mixed corpus can move it by fifteen. Spend your tuning time accordingly.

title: Agent Memory and State Management: A Practical Architecture Guide
dek: How you model agent state determines whether your system recovers gracefully or fails silently under pressure.

blocks.html:
Most agent failures I debug aren't model failures. The model knew what to do. The system just forgot what had already happened. A tool call succeeded on step three, but by step seven the agent had no reliable way to know that — so it called the tool again, wrote a duplicate record, and the user got billed twice. Memory wasn't a nice-to-have. It was load-bearing infrastructure that nobody designed.

Agent memory is one of those topics that gets compressed into a single word — "context" — as if that settles it. It doesn't. Context is just the immediate token window. Memory is everything else: what happened in previous turns, what the agent learned about the user or task, what intermediate results it produced, and what state the world is in right now. Conflating them is the first mistake most teams make when they move from a single-shot LLM call to a multi-step agent.

blocks.heading: Four Memory Scopes and What They're Actually For
blocks.alt: Comparison: Scope, What It Stores, Typical Medium

blocks.html:
The comparison above isn't theoretical taxonomy — it maps directly to where things break. In-context memory breaks when the window fills and you start truncating without a strategy. Episodic memory breaks when you restart a run after a crash and the agent has no idea where it left off. Semantic memory breaks when stale facts from six months ago override what the user just told you. Procedural memory — tracking actual side effects — breaks when you assume idempotency you never actually guaranteed. Each scope has its own failure mode, and each needs its own design decision.

The trickiest scope is procedural. Developers spend a lot of energy on what the agent knows and almost none on what the agent has done. But in any agent that takes real-world actions — sending messages, writing to databases, calling external APIs — you need a durable record of completed actions that survives process restarts. Without it, you get the double-execution bug I described above. The fix isn't clever prompting. It's checkpointing: persisting a state snapshot after every meaningful action so that resumption is safe and deterministic.

blocks.heading: Stateful Agent Execution Loop
blocks.alt: Receive Input → Load Checkpoint → Plan & Execute → Call Tools → Persist State → Return Output

blocks.html:
The flow above looks simple, but step two — "Load Checkpoint" — is where most implementations are underbuilt. A checkpoint needs to capture not just the message history but the full graph of what nodes have run, what tool calls completed successfully, and what the pending next step is. If your checkpoint is just a list of chat messages, you can reconstruct a conversation but you can't safely resume an interrupted task. Those are different requirements and they need different data models.

One design decision that comes up constantly in enterprise work: should memory be scoped to the user, the task, or the session? The answer is usually all three, layered. Session state is ephemeral and fast — it lives in memory or Redis and gets discarded when the run ends. Task state needs durability — it has to survive crashes and be queryable after the fact for auditing. User state needs careful governance — in regulated industries you may be legally required to let users inspect or delete what you've stored about them. Building a single monolithic "memory" object that serves all three purposes is a shortcut that creates problems you won't see until production.

blocks.label: The rule I enforce on every agent project
blocks.html: I require a written answer to three questions before any agent goes to staging: What state does it read at the start of each run? What state does it write, and when exactly? What happens if the process dies between those two moments? If the team can't answer all three, the agent isn't ready. Most of the time, this exercise surfaces a missing checkpoint or an implicit assumption about idempotency that would have caused a real incident within a week of launch.

project.note: Stateful agent graphs with built-in persistence and memory.

blocks.usage_note: I reach for LangGraph when an agent needs genuine persistence across runs — it gives me typed state schemas, built-in checkpointers, and a graph model that makes the execution path auditable, not just a chain of function calls I have to trace through logs.

code_example.code:
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, END
from langgraph.checkpoint.sqlite import SqliteSaver
from typing import TypedDict, Annotated
import operator

class TaskState(TypedDict):
    messages: Annotated[list, operator.add]
    completed_steps: Annotated[list, operator.add]
    user_id: str

def plan_node(state: TaskState) -> TaskState:
    last_msg = state["messages"][-1]
    plan = f"[Plan for: {last_msg}]"
    return {"messages": [plan], "completed_steps": []}

def execute_node(state: TaskState) -> TaskState:
    step_result = f"Executed step based on: {state['messages'][-1]}"
    return {
        "messages": [step_result],
        "completed_steps": ["execute"]
    }

def should_continue(state: TaskState) -> str:
    if "execute" in state["completed_steps"]:
        return END
    return "execute"

builder = StateGraph(TaskState)
builder.add_node("plan", plan_node)
builder.add_node("execute", execute_node)
builder.set_entry_point("plan")
builder.add_conditional_edges("plan", should_continue, {END: END, "execute": "execute"})
builder.add_edge("execute", END)

memory = SqliteSaver.from_conn_string(":memory:")
graph = builder.compile(checkpointer=memory)

config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "user-42-task-001"}}
result = graph.invoke(
    {"messages": ["Summarise Q2 sales data"], "completed_steps": [], "user_id": "user-42"},
    config=config
)
print(result)

title: Prompt Engineering Is a Skill, Not a Trick
dek: Most teams treat prompts as an afterthought. Here is why that costs them more than they think.

blocks.label: The claim I keep making to clients
blocks.html: Prompt engineering is not the "soft" part of an AI system. It is the specification. If your prompts are vague, your system is vague — and no amount of model upgrades will fix that.

Most teams treat prompt design the way they treat error messages: something you dash off once and never revisit. Then they wonder why the model behaves inconsistently in production, why outputs drift between model versions, why the same feature works in the demo and breaks for real users. The usual response is to blame the model. Swap in a newer one. Add more temperature tuning. What almost never happens is someone sitting down and actually reading the prompt critically — as a specification document — and asking whether it is precise enough to produce a deterministic class of outputs.

It is not. It almost never is. And that is the real problem.

The framing I use with every client is this: a prompt is a contract between you and the model. The model will honor the letter of that contract, not the spirit you had in mind when you wrote it. If your classification prompt says "label this as urgent if it seems important," you have not written a classifier — you have written a wish. The word "seems" is doing no work. "Important" is undefined. The model will fill in those blanks with something, and that something will shift depending on context, phrasing of the input, and which version of the model you are running against. Prompt optimization is the discipline of closing that gap: replacing ambiguity with precision, replacing intuition with tested structure.

This is also where the common advice to "just iterate until it works" breaks down. Iteration without measurement is superstition. You tweak a sentence, the output looks better on three examples, you ship it. Two weeks later a user hits the case you never tested and the whole thing falls apart. Real prompt optimization means defining what "correct" looks like before you start, building a small but representative eval set, and treating each prompt change like a code change — with a diff, a rationale, and a result.

The failure mode I see most often is not bad prompts — it is invisible prompts. The logic that should be in the prompt has been distributed across the application: some in a system message, some in a user message constructed at runtime, some implied by the few-shot examples, some assumed from the model's training. Nobody has a single document that says what this system is supposed to do. When something breaks, nobody knows where to look. The fix for this is not a better prompting technique — it is discipline about where decisions live. Write the full instruction set in one place. Make the examples explicit and curated, not grabbed at random. Treat the prompt as the source of truth for the model's behavior, because that is exactly what it is.

title: Fine-Tuning vs. Prompting: How to Choose Before You Commit
dek: A practical decision framework so you stop reaching for fine-tuning when a well-crafted prompt would do the job.

blocks.html: Most projects that end up in fine-tuning shouldn't be there. The pattern I see repeatedly: a team gets inconsistent output from a base model, concludes the model needs retraining, spends weeks curating examples and managing a training pipeline — and then discovers that a cleaner system prompt and a few well-chosen examples in context would have solved 90% of the problem. Fine-tuning isn't wrong; it's just expensive to undo once you're committed.

blocks.heading: Deciding Between Prompting and Fine-Tuning
blocks.alt: Define Target Behavior → Prototype with Prompts → Measure Gap → Gap Solvable? → Ship Prompt Solution → Build Fine-Tune Dataset

blocks.heading: When prompting is enough — check these first

items.title: The behavior is describable in words
items.detail: If you can write down the rule clearly, a system prompt can enforce it. Fine-tuning is for patterns too subtle or numerous to enumerate.

items.title: You need fewer than ~20 consistent output examples in context
items.detail: Few-shot prompting with good examples closes most format and style gaps without any training run.

items.title: Your use case is still changing
items.detail: Prompts iterate in minutes. Fine-tuned models lock you into a snapshot of requirements you had last month.

items.title: Latency and cost are not the bottleneck yet
items.detail: One valid reason to fine-tune is to shrink a long system prompt that runs on every request. Until that cost actually hurts, don't bother.

items.title: Style or tone that can't survive context length limits
items.detail: A brand voice requiring 2,000 words of examples per call is a genuine fine-tuning candidate — bake it into weights instead.

items.title: Consistent structured output at high volume
items.detail: If you're parsing model output programmatically at scale, a fine-tuned model that reliably hits your schema beats prompt engineering under pressure.

items.title: Proprietary domain knowledge the base model lacks
items.detail: Rare terminology, internal classification taxonomies, or specialized reasoning patterns that simply aren't in the pretraining data.

items.title: Latency-sensitive, prompt-heavy pipelines
items.detail: Fine-tuning a smaller model to match a larger one's prompted behavior is a legitimate optimization — once you've proven the behavior first.

title: Multi-Agent Orchestration: What Actually Breaks in Production
dek: Most agentic systems fail at coordination, not capability — here's how to build them so they don't.

blocks.html:
Every team I work with wants to build agents. Very few of them want to deal with what happens when two agents disagree on state, or when an LLM-driven router sends work to the wrong specialist for the fifth time in a row. That's the real problem with agentic workflows — not the individual agents, but the seams between them. Orchestration is where complexity compounds. A single agent with a clear task and a well-defined tool set is manageable. A crew of six agents sharing context through a poorly designed message bus is a debugging nightmare.

The practical split I use with clients is this: reach for CrewAI when you need to move fast and your workflow maps cleanly onto roles with defined responsibilities — a researcher, a writer, a reviewer. Reach for LangGraph when your workflow has conditional branches, loops, or human-in-the-loop checkpoints that need to survive a process restart. CrewAI abstracts the orchestration away from you, which is a gift until it isn't. LangGraph makes you draw the graph yourself, which is tedious until something goes wrong and you're grateful you can see exactly where execution stalled.

title: RAG in Practice: What Actually Breaks and Why
dek: How retrieval-augmented generation works in real enterprise deployments, including the failure modes nobody warns you about.

blocks.html:
A client called me six months into their internal knowledge-base project. They'd built a RAG system over their HR policy documents — about 800 PDFs — and it was confidently answering employee questions with information that had been superseded two policy cycles ago. The documents were in the index. The retrieval was working. The problem was subtler: they were chunking by page, so a chunk would contain the tail end of an old policy and the header of a new one, and the model would blend them into something that sounded authoritative but was factually wrong. Nobody had tested for that. That incident is basically my whole RAG education compressed into one phone call.

The idea behind RAG is straightforward — instead of baking all your knowledge into model weights (expensive, stale the moment training ends), you retrieve relevant text at query time and hand it to the model as context. The model reasons over fresh, specific information rather than interpolating from whatever it absorbed during pretraining. In principle this is elegant. In practice, the quality of your answers is almost entirely determined by decisions you make before the LLM ever sees a single token: how you chunk, what you embed, how you rank results, and whether your source data is actually clean.

from llama_index.core import VectorStoreIndex, SimpleDirectoryReader
from llama_index.core.node_parser import SentenceSplitter
from llama_index.llms.openai import OpenAI

Settings.llm = OpenAI(model="gpt-4o", temperature=0)
Settings.node_parser = SentenceSplitter(chunk_size=512, chunk_overlap=64)

index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(documents)

query_engine = index.as_query_engine(similarity_top_k=4)
response = query_engine.query(
    "What is the current parental leave entitlement for contractors?"
)

They may apply for unpaid leave under the general leave of absence policy,
subject to manager approval and a minimum 6-month tenure.

blocks.html:
The thing most teams underestimate is that RAG moves the complexity — it doesn't remove it. You've traded prompt engineering for data engineering, and data engineering is harder. Chunk boundaries matter enormously. Metadata filtering can make or break precision on large corpora. And retrieval ranking by cosine similarity alone will let you down whenever a user's question uses different vocabulary than your source documents. Hybrid search — combining dense embeddings with sparse keyword signals like BM25 — is almost always worth the extra setup once you're past the prototype stage. I've seen similarity scores look great in offline eval and still fail badly on real user queries, because real users don't phrase things the way policy writers do.

My honest advice: treat your chunking strategy as a first-class design decision, not a config value you set once and forget. Run evals against real queries before you go to production. And version your index — when source documents change, you need to know exactly which chunks changed with them, or you'll end up with the same call I got six months into that HR project.

blocks.text: RAG doesn't make your LLM smarter — it makes your data quality problems visible faster.

title: Prompt Caching: How to Stop Paying for the Same Tokens Twice
dek: A systematic look at prompt caching — what it actually saves, where it silently fails, and how to structure prompts to get real cost reductions.

blocks.html:
Token costs are not a rounding error at enterprise scale. A single RAG pipeline that prepends a 10,000-token system prompt to every user turn — running a few thousand times a day — can easily account for the majority of your monthly API bill. And the frustrating part is that most of those tokens are identical across requests: the same instructions, the same reference documents, the same few-shot examples, repeated verbatim every single time. You are paying full price to re-read the same book on every page turn.

Prompt caching is the fix for that specific problem. The idea is simple: the model provider caches the KV (key-value) state produced by processing a fixed prefix of your prompt, and on subsequent requests that share that same prefix, they skip recomputing it. Anthropic's implementation on Claude charges a one-time write cost (slightly above the normal input rate) and then a sharply reduced read cost — roughly 10% of standard input pricing — for every cache hit. The arithmetic is compelling, but only if you structure your prompts to actually hit the cache.

blocks.heading: How a Cache Hit Flows Through the API
blocks.alt: Request arrives → Prefix matched → KV state loaded → New tokens processed → Response generated

blocks.html:
The structural requirement is where most teams go wrong. Caching only works on a stable prefix — the cache key is the exact byte sequence of everything before your first dynamic content. That means your system prompt, your documents, your few-shot examples all need to come first, and the user's actual query needs to come last. If you are currently building prompts by appending context after the user message, or interpolating dynamic values anywhere inside your reference material, you are invalidating the cache on every request without knowing it. The provider isn't going to warn you. Your bill just stays high.

There is also the question of cache lifetime. On Claude, cached prefixes currently survive for approximately five minutes of inactivity — which is plenty for a busy production endpoint but completely useless for a low-traffic internal tool that gets one request every half hour. In that scenario you pay the write cost repeatedly and almost never recoup it with read savings. Before you instrument caching, you need an honest estimate of your request rate and the shape of your prompt. A 50,000-token shared context hitting the cache 200 times per hour is a very different proposition from a 2,000-token prompt hitting it twice a day.

blocks.heading: When Prompt Caching Actually Helps
blocks.alt: Comparison: Scenario, Good cache candidate, Poor cache candidate

blocks.html:
One pattern I reach for in document-heavy pipelines is what I think of as the frozen library approach. All reference material — policy documents, product specs, API schemas — gets concatenated into a single large block and placed immediately after the system prompt, before any conversation history. That block is never modified at runtime. The only thing that changes per request is the conversation tail. This keeps the cacheable prefix as large as possible and the dynamic suffix as small as possible. It does mean you have to be deliberate about document versioning: if you update one sentence in a 30-page policy doc, every cached prefix built on that doc is invalidated immediately.

The other failure mode worth naming is over-reliance on caching as a substitute for actual prompt engineering. I have seen teams pad their prompts with enormous retrieved chunks — far more than the model needs — because "caching makes it cheap." It does make the re-read cheap, but it does not make the initial write cheap, and it does not make the model better at finding the relevant needle in a larger haystack. Caching reduces the per-request cost of a fixed prefix; it does not fix a retrieval strategy that is dumping too much noise into context. Treat it as a cost efficiency tool, not a reason to abandon precision.

blocks.label: My rule for cache prefix design
blocks.html: In every project where I enable caching, I maintain a hard separation in the prompt-building code: a build_static_prefix() function that returns a deterministic string, and a build_dynamic_suffix() function that handles everything user-specific. The static function is unit-tested against a known hash — if the output changes unexpectedly, a test fails before the change reaches production. That discipline alone has saved me from several silent cache invalidations caused by someone innocently tweaking wording in a shared system prompt file.

project.note: Includes worked examples of prompt caching to cut latency and cost.

blocks.usage_note: I use the Claude Cookbooks caching example as a reference implementation when onboarding a new team to prompt caching — it shows the cache_control marker placement clearly and makes the before/after token accounting explicit.

code_example.code:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

# Static prefix — this is what gets cached.
# Must come before any dynamic content.
SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a contract analysis assistant.
The following is our standard supplier agreement template (v4.2).
Refer to it when answering questions about obligations and clauses.

[FULL CONTRACT TEXT — 8,000 tokens of legal boilerplate here]
"""

def ask_about_contract(user_question: str) -> str:
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-4-5",
        max_tokens=1024,
        system=[
            {
                "type": "text",
                "text": SYSTEM_PROMPT,
                "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"},  # mark the cacheable prefix
            }
        ],
        messages=[
            {"role": "user", "content": user_question}  # dynamic suffix stays outside
        ],
    )

    usage = response.usage
    print(f"Input tokens:        {usage.input_tokens}")
    print(f"Cache write tokens:  {getattr(usage, 'cache_creation_input_tokens', 0)}")
    print(f"Cache read tokens:   {getattr(usage, 'cache_read_input_tokens', 0)}")
    print(f"Output tokens:       {usage.output_tokens}")

    return response.content[0].text

# First call — pays the cache write cost once
print(ask_about_contract("What are the payment terms in section 4?"))

# Second call — prefix served from cache at ~10% of normal input cost
print(ask_about_contract("Does the agreement include an IP assignment clause?"))

title: Structured Outputs vs Tool Use: Know Which One You Actually Need
dek: Two ways to get reliable data out of an LLM — and picking the wrong one costs you more than you'd expect.

blocks.html:
Here's a distinction I have to draw for clients at least once a month: structured outputs and tool use are not the same thing, and they're not interchangeable. Structured outputs mean you constrain the model's response to a schema — JSON with specific fields, validated types, no freestyle prose. Tool use means you hand the model a callable interface and let it decide when and how to invoke it. Both give you machine-readable results. The similarity ends there.

The confusion is understandable. In practice, many demos blur the line — a function call that returns structured JSON, a schema that describes a tool's parameters. But the design decision underneath is real and has consequences. Structured outputs are about extraction and formatting. Tool use is about action and agency. If you pick the wrong one, you either build a rigid pipeline that can't handle edge cases, or you introduce an agent loop where a simple schema constraint would have been enough.

project.name: anthropics/claude-cookbooks
project.note: Tool-use and structured-output recipes (calculators, SQL, customer service agents).

blocks.usage_note: I reach for Claude's cookbook recipes when I need a concrete baseline for a client — they show the minimal viable version of each pattern without obscuring the trade-offs.

blocks.html:
That pattern — schema in the system prompt, parse the response — works well when the model's job is to read and reformat. It's predictable, cheap, and easy to validate. The failure mode is equally predictable: the moment you need the model to do something based on what it reads — query a database, call an API, branch on a condition — a static schema becomes a cage. You end up bolting conditional logic onto the output parser, which is exactly the wrong layer to put it in.

Tool use inverts the control flow. Instead of the model producing a final answer, it produces an intent — "call this function with these arguments" — and your code decides what to do with that intent. The model can call multiple tools in sequence, react to their return values, and reason across several steps. That's the genuine value. The cost is that you now have a loop, and loops have failure modes that a single-shot schema extraction doesn't: the model can call the wrong tool, call the right tool with bad arguments, or spin in a reasoning cycle that never terminates. You need retry logic, timeout handling, and ideally some kind of guardrail on the number of turns.

project.note: Reference MCP server implementations that expose tools to LLMs.

blocks.heading: Structured Outputs vs Tool Use
blocks.alt: Comparison: Aspect, Structured Outputs, Tool Use

blocks.html:
My rule of thumb: if you can write the business logic yourself and just need the model to fill in the blanks, use structured outputs. If the model needs information it doesn't have yet — information that lives in a system, a database, or an API — use tool use. The boundary is roughly "does the model need to reach out?" If yes, give it tools. If no, give it a schema.

One thing I'd push back on in how this space gets discussed: tool use is not automatically the more sophisticated choice. I've seen architectures where someone wired up six tools to answer a question that a well-prompted structured extraction would have handled in a single call. Every tool invocation is a round trip, a potential failure point, and added latency. Sometimes the smart move is the boring one.

title: MCP Is a Good Idea Wrapped in Too Much Hype
dek: Model Context Protocol solves a real coordination problem — but not the one most people think it does.

blocks.html: Every few months, the AI tooling world decides it has found the universal abstraction. MCP is the current candidate. The pitch sounds compelling: one protocol to rule all tool integrations, so your LLM can talk to your database, your calendar, your file system, and your internal APIs through a single, standardized interface. What I keep hearing from architects and developers is that MCP is going to eliminate the integration problem entirely. That claim is wrong, and believing it will cost you time.

blocks.label: What MCP actually solves
blocks.html: MCP doesn't eliminate integration complexity — it moves it. You still have to build, host, and maintain every server. What you gain is a standard shape for that work, which matters most when you're composing tools from multiple teams or vendors, not when you're wiring up a single internal service.

Here is what MCP genuinely does well: it gives tool authors and model orchestrators a shared contract. Before that existed, every agent framework invented its own tool-calling convention. LangChain did it one way, AutoGen another, raw OpenAI function-calling a third. If you wanted the same tool available across two frameworks, you wrote glue code. MCP replaces that glue with a spec. That is real value — narrow, but real. The failure mode I see in enterprise projects right now is teams treating MCP as if the protocol itself does the hard part. It doesn't. Deciding what a tool should expose, what its error surface looks like, how it handles auth, how it behaves when the underlying service is slow — none of that is answered by the protocol. You still make every one of those decisions. You just make them inside a standardized wrapper.

The other thing worth saying plainly: MCP's value scales with the number of consumers, not the number of servers. If you have one agent and three internal tools, a bespoke integration is probably faster to ship and easier to debug than standing up three MCP servers with proper transport layers. The protocol pays off when you have a tool that ten different agents or products need to call, or when you're publishing something to the broader ecosystem and you want it to work with whatever orchestration layer your customers already run. That's a legitimate use case. It's just a narrower one than the hype suggests. Anthropic built MCP, and they are clearly betting that a thriving third-party server ecosystem emerges around it — the same way npm or VS Code extensions created compounding value over time. That bet might pay off. But the ecosystem isn't there yet, and in the meantime, most teams are writing MCP servers for tools they could have exposed as a plain HTTP endpoint in an afternoon.

title: How to Build a Real Evaluation Pipeline for LLM Systems
dek: Skip the vibe checks — here's a concrete process for testing LLM outputs you can actually trust.

blocks.html: Most teams I talk to are evaluating their LLM systems the same way: they run a few prompts, it looks reasonable, and they ship. That works until it doesn't — and when it breaks in production, they have no baseline to diff against. A proper eval pipeline isn't complicated, but it does require committing to a specific sequence of steps before you touch a model setting or swap a prompt.

blocks.heading: LLM Evaluation Pipeline
blocks.alt: Define Test Cases → Run Model → Score Outputs → Store Results → Compare Baselines → Ship or Iterate

blocks.heading: Rules for Building a Test Suite That Actually Holds Up

items.title: Cover failure modes, not happy paths
items.detail: Your golden dataset should include adversarial inputs, edge cases, and real user queries that caused problems — not just the clean examples where the model already does well.

items.title: Separate deterministic from model-graded checks
items.detail: Use exact-match or regex assertions for anything structural (JSON schema, required fields, citation format). Reserve LLM-as-judge only for subjective quality where no ground truth exists.

items.title: Version your evals alongside your prompts
items.detail: If you change a prompt and don't update the eval, your scores are measuring the old behavior. Treat evals as first-class code in the same repo, same PR.

items.title: Set a regression threshold before you run
items.detail: Decide in advance what score drop counts as a regression — 2%, 5%, whatever fits your risk tolerance. If you decide after seeing results, you're rationalizing, not evaluating.

project.name: openai/evals
project.note: Framework and open registry of benchmarks for evaluating LLM systems.

blocks.usage_note: I use openai/evals to register a custom eval against a fixed dataset and get reproducible scores I can track across model versions.

code_example.code:
# my_evals/summarization_quality.yaml
id: summarization-quality-v1
description: Evaluates factual accuracy of summaries against source documents
metrics: [accuracy]

eval:
  id: summarization-quality-v1
  metrics: [accuracy]

samples:
  type: jsonl
  path: data/summarization_samples.jsonl

completion_fns:
  - oaieval:gpt-4o

eval_class: evals.elsuite.modelgraded.classify:ModelGradedClassify
args:
  prompt_template: prompts/factual_accuracy.jinja2
  choice_strings: [correct, incorrect, partial]
  eval_type: classify

Samples: 120
Accuracy: 0.847
Correct: 101 / 120
Partial: 12 / 120
Incorrect: 7 / 120
Final report written to: /tmp/evallogs/summarization-quality-v1.json

items.title: Check score distribution, not just the mean
items.detail: A 0.85 average faithfulness score can hide a cluster of 0.3s on a specific query type. Look at the tail before declaring success.

items.title: Re-run on a held-out slice monthly
items.detail: Model drift and prompt drift are real. A score that was fine in January may have quietly degraded by March with no deployment on your side.

items.title: Document what each metric does and doesn't capture
items.detail: Faithfulness doesn't catch hallucinations about things not in the retrieved context. Know the blind spots of every metric you report.

title: Stop Trusting LLM Output — Validate It Like Any Other API
dek: Guardrails belong in your code, not in your prompt. Here's how to enforce them.

blocks.html: Most teams I work with spend weeks iterating on system prompts, trying to get the model to behave. The model returns valid JSON — until it doesn't. It stays on topic — until a user asks something slightly sideways. Treating prompt engineering as your only line of defense is the wrong mental model. An LLM is a stochastic external service, and you wouldn't skip input validation on any other external API. The same discipline applies here.

The practical move is to validate at the boundary: after the model responds, before that response touches anything else in your system. That means checking structure (did we get the fields we expected?), checking content (is anything in here that shouldn't be?), and deciding what happens on failure — retry, fallback, or surface an error. The failure path is the part most teams skip, and it's exactly where production incidents come from. A validator that raises an exception and crashes your pipeline is only marginally better than no validator at all.

project.name: guardrails-ai/guardrails
project.note: Input/output guards to detect and mitigate LLM risks, and enforce structure.

blocks.usage_note: I reach for guardrails-ai when I need both schema enforcement and content policy checks in one place, without wiring up three separate libraries.

code_example.code:
import guardrails as gd
from guardrails.hub import RegexMatch, ValidLength
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class ProductSummary(BaseModel):
    name: str = Field(
        validators=[ValidLength(min=2, max=80, on_fail="reask")]
    )
    one_liner: str = Field(
        validators=[
            ValidLength(min=10, max=160, on_fail="reask"),
            RegexMatch(regex=r"^[^<>{}]+$", on_fail="filter"),
        ]
    )
    price_usd: float

guard = gd.Guard.from_pydantic(ProductSummary, num_reasks=2)

raw_llm_output = '{"name": "Noise Pro", "one_liner": "Studio-quality sound, zero cables.", "price_usd": 149.0}'

result = guard.parse(raw_llm_output)
print(result.validated_output)

title: What a Production Incident Taught Me About LLM Tracing
dek: When your LLM pipeline breaks silently, you need traces — not logs, not vibes.

blocks.html:
Three weeks into a client engagement, their document processing pipeline started returning garbage. Not errors — garbage. The LLM was responding, latency looked fine on the dashboard, and yet the outputs were subtly wrong in ways that took a human reviewer two days to even notice. We had logging. We had token counts. What we didn't have was any visibility into which prompt had been sent, what the retrieved context looked like at that exact moment, or how the chain of calls had composed itself. We were debugging a multi-step system by staring at its final output, which is roughly like diagnosing an engine problem by looking at the exhaust.

That incident is why I now treat tracing as non-negotiable on any LLM system that touches production. Not a nice-to-have, not something you retrofit after the first incident — something you wire in before you write the first prompt template.

project.name: langfuse/langfuse
project.note: Open-source LLM observability platform: tracing, evals, prompt management.

blocks.usage_note: I reach for Langfuse when I need a self-hostable, open-source tracing layer that gives me full span-level visibility into every LLM call, retrieval step, and chain branch without sending client data to a third-party cloud.
blocks.example_output:
Trace created: https://cloud.langfuse.com/trace/a3f9c12e
  └─ process_document          [823ms]
      ├─ retrieve_relevant_chunks [112ms]  doc_id=doc-42
      └─ generate_summary          [701ms]  tokens=in:87 out:54  model=gpt-4o-mini

What makes the decorator approach worth it is the nesting. Every call to retrieve_relevant_chunks and generate_summary shows up as a child span under the parent trace, so when something goes wrong at 2am you can pull up a single trace ID and see exactly what prompt text hit the model, what the retrieval returned, how long each step took, and what the model said back. Compare that to grepping through flat log files across three services. The difference isn't convenience — it's the difference between finding the bug in ten minutes versus two days, as I learned the hard way.

One thing I want to flag that people underestimate: tracing isn't just for debugging. Once you have spans with input/output captured, you can run evals against historical traces, catch prompt regressions before they reach users, and actually measure whether a prompt change improved things or just moved the failure mode. Langfuse's eval and prompt management features sit on top of the same trace data, which means the observability layer doubles as your experimentation infrastructure. That's a lot of leverage from one integration.

blocks.text: If you can't replay exactly what your LLM saw and said, you don't have a production system — you have a production guess.

title: Red-Teaming LLM Systems Before Your Users Do It for You
dek: How to run structured adversarial testing on prompts, agents, and RAG pipelines — and what to do with what you find.

blocks.html:
Most AI systems I audit in enterprise settings have never been deliberately attacked by the people who built them. They've been tested for correctness — does the chatbot answer the right question? — but not for failure modes that only appear when someone is actively trying to break things. That gap is where red-teaming lives, and closing it is not optional if you're deploying anything that touches real users or real data.

Red-teaming in the LLM context means deliberately probing a system with adversarial inputs: prompt injections, jailbreak attempts, data exfiltration vectors, role-confusion attacks, and inputs designed to make the model contradict its own instructions or reveal information it shouldn't. The goal isn't to find every possible bug — it's to find the categories of failure your system is structurally vulnerable to, so you can address them before someone else does.

There's a common misconception worth addressing directly: red-teaming is not the same as evaluation. Evaluation tells you how well a model performs on a distribution of expected inputs. Adversarial testing tells you what happens at the edges — and at the edges is where trust breaks. A RAG pipeline that summarizes documents beautifully 98% of the time can still be coaxed into ignoring its retrieval context entirely and hallucinating confidently if the right instruction appears in a retrieved chunk. That's a prompt injection via the retrieval path, and standard evals will never surface it.

The other thing I push back on is the idea that this is a one-time exercise. System prompts change. New tools get added to agents. The underlying model gets swapped or fine-tuned. Each of those changes reopens attack surface. Red-teaming needs to be part of your deployment pipeline, not a checkbox you tick before launch.

blocks.heading: Adversarial Testing Pipeline
blocks.alt: Define Threat Model → Generate Attack Probes → Run Against System → Score & Classify → Patch & Retest

blocks.html: A useful threat model for an LLM system covers at least four categories. First, prompt injection — inputs that attempt to override or hijack the system prompt, whether they arrive via the user turn or through retrieved content. Second, information leakage — probes that try to extract the system prompt itself, internal tool schemas, or data from other users' sessions. Third, policy bypass — attempts to get the model to produce content it's been instructed to refuse, typically through roleplay framing, hypothetical framing, or persona switching. Fourth, behavioral drift — inputs that don't look adversarial at all but gradually shift the model's behavior over a long conversation. That last category is the hardest to catch with automated tools and often requires human red-teamers.

blocks.heading: Manual vs. Automated Red-Teaming
blocks.alt: Comparison: Aspect, Manual Red-Teaming, Automated Scanning

blocks.html:
In practice I run both. Automated scanning — using tools like promptfoo — catches the known vulnerability classes every time a system prompt changes or a new tool is wired into an agent. Manual sessions, which I run with a small group of people who genuinely enjoy breaking things, surface the weird stuff: the multi-step social engineering sequences, the attacks that require understanding the business context, the edge cases that no template library has thought of yet. The automated pass tells me the floor; the manual pass tells me what I don't know I don't know.

One thing I've learned the hard way: the quality of your attack probes determines everything. Generic jailbreak lists from GitHub are table stakes — any well-configured system should handle those. What actually matters is building probes that are specific to your system's context. If you're building a legal document assistant, your red-team probes should include attempts to get legal advice, attempts to extract client data mentioned in retrieved documents, and attempts to impersonate the system's persona in ways that could mislead a real user. Generic probes won't tell you whether your specific deployment is safe.

blocks.label: The probe library I actually maintain
blocks.html: For every production deployment I run, I keep a versioned YAML file of adversarial probes that are specific to that system — its domain, its tools, its known sensitive data categories. It starts small, maybe 30-40 probes, and grows every time a real user does something unexpected or a manual red-team session surfaces a new pattern. That file runs in CI on every system prompt change. It's not glamorous, but it's caught three serious regressions in the past year that would have shipped to production otherwise.

title: More Context Is Not the Same as Better Context
dek: Everyone is racing to stuff more tokens into the window. That is not context engineering.

blocks.html: The 1M-token context window is now a selling point. Tencent ships Hy4 with one. Gemini had one first. OpenAI is closing the gap. And every time a new model drops with a larger window, I watch enterprise teams immediately treat it as permission to stop thinking — just throw the whole document corpus in and let the model sort it out. That instinct is wrong, and it is costing people real money and real quality.

blocks.label: The claim I'll defend here
blocks.html: A 1M-token context window does not make context engineering easier. It makes sloppy context engineering harder to notice — until it fails at scale, in production, on the case that actually matters.

Context engineering is the discipline of deciding what information the model needs, in what form, and in what order — not how much you can physically fit. Those are completely different problems. When you dump 800 pages of policy documents into a prompt because you technically can, you are not doing context engineering. You are doing context avoidance. The model will still answer, often plausibly, and you will not immediately see the failure mode: the relevant clause buried on page 340 that gets drowned out by the surrounding noise, the instruction at position 200K that the model effectively ignores because of well-documented mid-context attention degradation, the cost of re-sending that same static corpus on every single call.

Good context engineering looks nothing like that. It looks like asking: which parts of this information are truly dynamic per request, and which parts are stable enough to cache? What is the retrieval strategy — do I need a sub-agent to pull specific sections rather than flooding the root context? Is the structure of the information helping the model locate what matters, or is it just raw text poured in? These are architectural decisions, not token-budget decisions. The window size is a constraint to work within, not a design philosophy.

The practical failure mode I see most often is what I call context dilution: the signal-to-noise ratio in the prompt drops so far that the model starts hedging, averaging across conflicting information, or simply missing the specific detail the user actually needed. You can have 900K tokens in the window and still give the model less usable information than a tightly curated 10K prompt would. That is not a model problem. That is an architecture problem, and no future model release will fix it for you — because the model is doing exactly what you asked. You asked it to process everything. It processed everything. The answer just came out wrong.

The discipline worth building is not "how do I use the full context window" but "how do I design the information flow so the model receives the right context at the right moment, and nothing else." That means chunking and retrieval strategies, prompt caching for static content, sub-agent decomposition for large document sets, and deliberate ordering of instructions relative to content. It is more work than dumping a PDF. It is also the only approach that holds up when the stakes are real.

title: Dense Retrieval vs. Structured Indexing: Picking Your Embedding Strategy
dek: Two tools, two philosophies — here's how to choose the right embedding approach for your production retrieval system.

blocks.html:
Most teams I work with arrive at the same fork in the road: they know they need semantic search, they've heard about embeddings, and they've picked a model. Then comes the real decision — do you build a lean vector store and own the retrieval logic yourself, or do you use a higher-level indexing framework that abstracts the whole pipeline? These aren't just different libraries. They encode different assumptions about where complexity should live.

The honest answer is that neither approach is universally better. A bare-metal embedding database gives you precision and predictability at the cost of more wiring. A framework like LlamaIndex gives you speed and composability at the cost of opacity. I've run both in production. What follows is the actual trade-off, not the marketing version.

project.name: chroma-core/chroma
project.note: Embedding database and search infrastructure for AI applications.

blocks.usage_note: I reach for Chroma when I want the retrieval layer to be exactly as thin as I design it — no hidden re-ranking, no surprise chunking, just vectors in and results out.

code_example.code:
import chromadb
from chromadb.utils import embedding_functions

client = chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./chroma_store")

ef = embedding_functions.SentenceTransformerEmbeddingFunction(
    model_name="all-MiniLM-L6-v2"
)

collection = client.get_or_create_collection(
    name="support_tickets",
    embedding_function=ef,
    metadata={"hnsw:space": "cosine"}
)

collection.add(
    documents=[
        "Login fails after password reset on mobile",
        "Invoice PDF does not render in Safari",
        "Two-factor auth code arrives 5 minutes late",
    ],
    ids=["t001", "t002", "t003"]
)

results = collection.query(
    query_texts=["user cannot sign in after changing password"],
    n_results=2
)

print(results["documents"])
print(results["distances"])

[[0.112, 0.431]]

blocks.html:
Chroma's model is deliberately minimal. You supply documents, it stores vectors, you query and get distances back. That transparency is a genuine advantage when you need to instrument or debug retrieval — you can inspect every step. The downside is that you're also responsible for chunking strategy, metadata filtering design, and any re-ranking you want on top. None of that is hard, but it adds up. A client once asked me why their retrieval quality dropped after they updated their documents. The answer was a chunking change upstream — something a framework might have caught, but that Chroma happily ignored because Chroma doesn't know or care about your chunking.

LlamaIndex takes the opposite stance. It treats the entire pipeline — loading, chunking, embedding, indexing, querying, even synthesizing an answer — as one composable system. That's genuinely useful when you're building fast or when your data comes from heterogeneous sources. The risk is that defaults hide a lot of behavior. I've seen teams spend days debugging retrieval quality problems that turned out to be caused by LlamaIndex's default chunk size of 1024 tokens combined with a context window that was already under pressure. The abstraction saved them a week on day one and cost them two weeks on day thirty.

project.note: Indexing and retrieval framework built on top of embeddings.

from llama_index.core import VectorStoreIndex, SimpleDirectoryReader, Settings
from llama_index.embeddings.huggingface import HuggingFaceEmbedding
from llama_index.core.node_parser import SentenceSplitter

Settings.embed_model = HuggingFaceEmbedding(model_name="BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5")
Settings.node_parser = SentenceSplitter(chunk_size=512, chunk_overlap=64)
Settings.llm = None

documents = SimpleDirectoryReader("./policy_docs").load_data()

index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(documents, show_progress=True)

retriever = index.as_retriever(similarity_top_k=3)
nodes = retriever.retrieve("What is the data retention policy for EU customers?")

for node in nodes:

    print(node.text[:120])

blocks.html: The practical rule I've landed on: if your retrieval logic is the core of the product — if the quality of search directly determines whether the thing works — start with Chroma or a similarly thin store. Own the pipeline. If retrieval is infrastructure for something else, like a document Q&A feature that needs to ship in two weeks, LlamaIndex's defaults are probably good enough to get you there, and you can always swap the underlying store later. What I'd avoid is the middle path: using a framework but fighting its abstractions at every step. That's the worst of both worlds.

title: How to Give Your Agents Memory That Actually Persists
dek: A concrete guide to structuring agent state so it survives across turns, sessions, and restarts.

blocks.html: Most agent failures I diagnose aren't reasoning failures — they're memory failures. The agent answered the right question, then forgot the context by the next turn. Or it accumulated state in a plain Python dict that evaporated the moment the process restarted. Getting memory right is mostly an architecture decision, not a model decision.

blocks.heading: Agent Memory Lifecycle
blocks.alt: User Input → Load State → Run Agent → Update State → Persist State → Return Output

blocks.heading: Rules for Agent State That Doesn't Bite You

items.title: Separate ephemeral from persistent state
items.detail: Scratch-pad reasoning and tool call results belong in short-term state. User preferences, past decisions, and accumulated facts need to hit a real store — SQLite, Postgres, Redis — before the turn ends.

items.title: Use a thread ID from the start
items.detail: Every conversation or task run gets a unique thread ID. Pass it through every layer. Adding it later, when you need cross-session memory, is painful.

items.title: Version your state schema
items.detail: State shapes change as you add features. A schema migration story needs to exist before you hit production — not after you have 50,000 stale checkpoints.

items.title: Cap what you carry forward
items.detail: Unbounded message history will eventually exceed your context window or slow your persistence layer. Summarize or prune at a defined threshold — 20 messages is a reasonable starting point.

items.title: Test memory in isolation
items.detail: Write unit tests that serialize state, reload it cold, and verify the agent continues correctly. Most memory bugs only appear on the second or third turn.

project.name: langchain-ai/langgraph
project.note: Stateful agent graphs with built-in persistence and memory.

blocks.usage_note: LangGraph is my default choice when an agent needs real persistence — its checkpointer abstraction means I swap between in-memory and Postgres without touching graph logic.

code_example.code:
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, END
from langgraph.checkpoint.sqlite import SqliteSaver
from typing import TypedDict, List

class AgentState(TypedDict):
    messages: List[str]
    user_name: str
    turn_count: int

def greet(state: AgentState) -> AgentState:
    name = state["user_name"]
    count = state["turn_count"] + 1
    reply = f"Turn {count}: Hello again, {name}." if count > 1 else f"Nice to meet you, {name}."
    return {"messages": state["messages"] + [reply], "turn_count": count}

builder = StateGraph(AgentState)
builder.add_node("greet", greet)
builder.set_entry_point("greet")
builder.add_edge("greet", END)

memory = SqliteSaver.from_conn_string("checkpoints.db")
graph = builder.compile(checkpointer=memory)

thread = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "user-42"}}
result = graph.invoke({"messages": [], "user_name": "Elena", "turn_count": 0}, thread)
print(result["messages"][-1])

# Second invocation — state is reloaded from SQLite automatically
result2 = graph.invoke({"messages": result["messages"], "user_name": "Elena", "turn_count": result["turn_count"]}, thread)
print(result2["messages"][-1])

blocks.example_output:
Nice to meet you, Elena.
Turn 2: Hello again, Elena.

blocks.html: The checkpointer is doing the heavy lifting here — every time graph.invoke completes, the full state is written to SQLite against that thread ID. Swap SqliteSaver for AsyncPostgresSaver in production and nothing else changes. The part people underestimate is the state schema itself: keep it flat, keep it serializable, and resist the urge to stuff live objects or closures into it.

title: Write Better Prompts by Reading Anthropic's Own Work
dek: Prompt engineering has real structure — steal from the people who test it most.

blocks.html: Most prompt engineering advice is circular. "Be specific." "Give examples." "Use clear instructions." True, but useless without a concrete reference point for what good actually looks like in production. The fastest way I've improved my prompting over the past year isn't reading papers — it's reading working examples written by people who test against real models every day. Anthropic's public system prompts are one source. Their Claude Cookbooks repository is a better one for practitioners.

The pattern that shows up repeatedly in well-engineered prompts: role before task, constraints before examples, and output format specified last. Get that order wrong and you waste tokens on corrections or, worse, you get plausible-looking output that silently misses the intent. The other thing worth noticing in the cookbook examples is what's not there — no padding, no excessive politeness, no hedge phrases like "please try to." Every word is load-bearing. That's the discipline most enterprise prompts lack, and it's exactly where quality degrades at scale when prompts get passed between team members and accumulate noise.

project.name: anthropics/claude-cookbooks
project.note: Worked prompt-design examples across classification, RAG, and summarization.

blocks.usage_note: I reach for the cookbooks repo when a client needs a classification or summarization prompt fast — the patterns are already validated and I can adapt rather than start from scratch.

code_example.code:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

system_prompt = """
You are a document classifier for a financial services firm.
Your task: assign exactly one category to the document excerpt below.

Categories:
- COMPLIANCE: regulatory requirements, audit trails, policy adherence
- RISK: exposure assessment, loss scenarios, counterparty concerns
- OPERATIONS: process documentation, system outages, workflow issues
- OTHER: anything that does not clearly fit the above

Rules:
- Output only the category label, nothing else.
- If the excerpt is ambiguous, choose the closest match.
- Do not explain your reasoning.
"""

document = """
The settlement failure on 14 March affected three counterparties.
Back-office reconciliation is pending sign-off from the risk desk.
"""

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-4-5",
    max_tokens=16,
    system=system_prompt,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": document}]
)

print(response.content[0].text)

title: Fine-Tuning Is Not a Prompt That Scales
dek: When to stop fighting your base model with clever prompts and actually commit to fine-tuning.

blocks.html: A client came to me last autumn with a formatting problem. Their model — GPT-4o, well-prompted — kept producing summaries that were almost right. The structure was close, the tone was close, but the output never quite matched the internal report format their analysts expected. So they'd iterated. A system prompt that was now 1,400 words long, three few-shot examples, a separate validation step that re-asked the model to self-correct. It worked about 80% of the time. They wanted to get to 95%. My first instinct was to reach for a smarter prompt. My second instinct — the right one — was to ask how long they'd already been doing this. Eighteen months, they said. That's when I told them prompting had already lost this particular fight.

The honest version of the fine-tuning vs. prompting decision is this: prompting is renting behaviour from a model, and fine-tuning is buying it. Renting is cheaper upfront and flexible — you can change what you want on a Tuesday without touching any infrastructure. But if you're renting the same behaviour every single day, at scale, with a 1,400-word lease agreement you have to re-negotiate on every API call, the economics and reliability both start to crack. Fine-tuning bakes consistent behaviour into the weights. You pay once (in data curation time and training cost), and the model just knows what you want. The failure mode people don't talk about enough: fine-tuning on too little data, or on data that doesn't actually reflect the edge cases that matter, gives you a model that's confidently wrong in a narrower range of ways. It's not a free upgrade — it's a different set of trade-offs.

project.name: anthropics/claude-cookbooks
project.note: Examples showing when prompting/tool use suffice vs. when they don't.

blocks.usage_note: I use the Claude cookbooks repo as a concrete reference when I need to show a client exactly where the prompting ceiling is — the examples make the boundary visible without me having to argue theory.

code_example.code:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

# Scenario: strict output schema — a classic prompting-vs-fine-tuning stress test
SYSTEM_PROMPT = """
You are a financial report formatter.
Always return JSON matching this exact schema:
{"summary": str, "risk_level": "low"|"medium"|"high", "flags": [str]}
No extra keys. No prose outside the JSON object.
"""

raw_text = """
Q3 revenue missed targets by 12%. Currency hedging partially offset losses.
Two regulatory inquiries opened in Germany. Cash reserves remain stable.
"""

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-4-5",
    max_tokens=512,
    system=SYSTEM_PROMPT,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"Format this report:\n{raw_text}"}]
)

print(response.content[0].text)

blocks.html: That code works. Most of the time. But run it across a thousand varied documents — some poorly formatted, some ambiguous, some in mixed languages — and you'll start seeing schema violations, extra prose bleeding in, risk levels that don't match what a domain expert would assign. A well-prompted Claude is genuinely good at following instructions, which is exactly why it can fool you into thinking you're done when you're not. The signal that you've crossed into fine-tuning territory isn't usually a catastrophic failure. It's a slow accumulation of edge cases that your prompt keeps getting patched to handle, each patch making the next failure slightly more exotic. If you're on patch number seven, stop patching. Curate 200-500 high-quality examples of the exact behaviour you want, fine-tune, and get off the treadmill.

blocks.text: If your prompt has grown longer than a short-story and you're still negotiating with the model, you've already decided — you just haven't admitted it yet.
